_schema.description: Clinical rule base for PTB-XL ECG super-classes. Each entry is the ONLY authorised source of facts for the generated report. Rules are generic, educational descriptions of standard ECG findings; they are NOT patient-specific medical advice.
_schema.disclaimer: Research and demonstration only. Not for clinical diagnosis. Any ECG interpretation must be confirmed by a qualified clinician.

entries.name: Normal ECG
entries.description: The recording shows no abnormality among the diagnostic categories covered by this system. Rhythm, conduction intervals, QRS morphology and repolarisation all fall within expected limits.
entries.ecg_signs: Regular sinus rhythm with a P wave preceding each QRS complex, normal PR and QRS durations, and no significant ST-segment or T-wave deviation.
entries.urgency: No urgency indicated by this recording alone.
entries.action: No ECG-driven action required. Clinical assessment still governs management, since a normal ECG does not exclude all cardiac conditions.

entries.name: Myocardial infarction
entries.description: Findings consistent with myocardial infarction, meaning heart muscle damage caused by interrupted blood supply. The pattern may reflect an acute event or an older, healed infarction.
entries.ecg_signs: Pathological Q waves, loss of R-wave progression across the chest leads, and ST-segment or T-wave changes in a territorial distribution matching a coronary artery.
entries.urgency: High priority. An acute infarction is a medical emergency; a prior infarction is not acute but carries ongoing cardiovascular risk.
entries.action: Correlate immediately with symptoms, timing and cardiac biomarkers. Seek urgent cardiology assessment if the presentation is acute.

entries.name: ST/T change
entries.description: Abnormalities of the repolarisation phase, when the ventricles recover after contracting. These changes are sensitive but not specific: they may reflect ischaemia, electrolyte disturbance, drug effect or strain.
entries.ecg_signs: ST-segment depression or elevation, T-wave flattening or inversion, and other deviations of the ST segment or T wave from the baseline.
entries.urgency: Moderate priority. Significance depends heavily on the clinical context and on whether the changes are new.
entries.action: Compare with any previous ECG to determine whether the change is new. Correlate with symptoms, electrolytes and medication, and seek cardiology advice where ischaemia is suspected.

entries.name: Conduction disturbance
entries.description: Impaired propagation of the electrical impulse through the heart's conduction system. Depending on the level of the block, the delay may be benign or may threaten adequate ventricular activation.
entries.ecg_signs: Prolonged PR interval, widened QRS complex, bundle branch block morphology, or dropped beats where a P wave is not followed by a QRS complex.
entries.urgency: Variable. Isolated first-degree or bundle branch block is often benign; high-grade or complete block requires urgent attention.
entries.action: Determine the level and degree of the block. Review rate-slowing medication, and seek urgent cardiology assessment for high-grade block or symptoms such as syncope.

entries.name: Hypertrophy
entries.description: Voltage and morphology criteria suggesting thickening or enlargement of a cardiac chamber, most often the left ventricle. This usually reflects chronic pressure or volume overload rather than an acute event.
entries.ecg_signs: Increased QRS voltage meeting established hypertrophy criteria, often with a strain pattern of ST depression and T-wave inversion in the lateral leads, and left axis deviation.
entries.urgency: Low urgency on the ECG alone, but it signals an underlying condition that merits investigation.
entries.action: Investigate the underlying cause, typically hypertension or valvular disease. Confirm chamber size with echocardiography, since ECG voltage criteria have limited accuracy.
